questions.stem: What is the concentration of a solution made by dissolving 0.500 mol of sodium chloride in water to make 250 mL of solution?
questions.explanation: c = n/V with V in litres: 0.500/0.250 = 2.00 mol/L. Multiplying n by V gives 0.125, and using 250 instead of 0.250 L gives 0.00200.

questions.stem: What is the concentration of a solution containing 4.00 g of sodium hydroxide (M = 40.0 g/mol) in 500 mL of solution?
questions.explanation: n = 4.00/40.0 = 0.100 mol, and c = 0.100/0.500 = 0.200 mol/L. 0.100 is the number of moles, not the concentration.

questions.stem: A hydrochloric acid solution has a concentration of 0.150 mol/L. What is its concentration in g/L (M(HCl) = 36.5 g/mol)?
questions.explanation: Multiply the concentration in mol/L by the molar mass: 0.150 × 36.5 = 5.48 g/L. Dividing instead gives 0.00411, which is far too small.

questions.stem: A sodium carbonate solution contains 21.2 g/L of Na₂CO₃ (M = 106.0 g/mol). What is its concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Divide the concentration in g/L by the molar mass: 21.2/106.0 = 0.200 mol/L. Multiplying gives 2250, and 106.0/21.2 = 5.00 is the division the wrong way round.

questions.stem: What mass of hydrogen chloride is dissolved in 250 mL of 0.200 mol/L hydrochloric acid (M(HCl) = 36.5 g/mol)?
questions.explanation: n = c × V = 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol, and m = 0.0500 × 36.5 = 1.83 g. 7.30 g is the mass in a full litre, and 0.0500 is the amount in moles, not grams.

questions.stem: What is the formula of nitric acid?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid is HNO₃. NH₃ is ammonia, a base, and H₂SO₄ is sulfuric acid.

questions.stem: Which acid is found in vinegar?
questions.explanation: Vinegar is a dilute solution of ethanoic (acetic) acid. Citric acid is the acid found in lemons and other citrus fruit.

questions.stem: Which property is typical of bases in aqueous solution?
options: They taste sour and turn blue litmus red
They react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide
They react with magnesium to release hydrogen
They feel slippery and turn red litmus blue
questions.explanation: Bases feel slippery (soapy) and turn red litmus blue. A sour taste, turning blue litmus red and reacting with carbonates and reactive metals are properties of acids. Never taste or touch laboratory chemicals.

questions.stem: Hydrogen chloride is a covalent gas, yet its solution in water conducts electricity and is acidic. Why?
options: Water molecules donate protons to the HCl molecules
Its molecules dissolve unchanged and carry charge
Its molecules donate protons to water, forming ions in solution
Its molecules are already ions in the gas phase
questions.explanation: Some covalent molecules, such as HCl, ionise when they dissolve, donating H⁺ and leaving Cl⁻ in solution. The ions carry the current and the H⁺ makes the solution acidic; ammonia is a notable covalent molecule that gives a basic solution instead.

questions.stem: How does the Brønsted-Lowry model define an acid?
questions.explanation: A Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton (H⁺ ion) and a base accepts one. Defining acids by hydroxide ions or electrons is not this model.

questions.stem: In the reaction NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), which species acts as the Brønsted-Lowry base?
questions.explanation: Ammonia gains a proton from HCl to become NH₄⁺, so ammonia is the proton acceptor, the base. HCl donates the proton, so it is the acid.

questions.stem: Using hydrogen ions, which equation shows hydrochloric acid acting as an acid in water?
questions.explanation: HCl donates a proton, so it ionises into H⁺ and Cl⁻. Hydrogen loses its electron to chlorine, which is why the hydrogen ion is positive and the chloride ion negative.

questions.stem: Ammonia dissolves in water: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). What role does water play?
options: It donates a hydroxide ion, so it acts as a base
It only dissolves the ammonia and does not react
It donates a proton, so it acts as an acid
It accepts a proton, so it acts as a base
questions.explanation: Water gives a proton to ammonia and becomes OH⁻, so here it is the proton donor, the acid. The hydroxide ions formed make the solution basic.

questions.stem: Which statement about ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, is correct?
options: It is not an acid, because its molecules contain carbon
It is monoprotic: only one of its four hydrogens can be donated
It is tetraprotic: all four of its hydrogens can be donated
It is diprotic: the two hydrogens bonded to oxygen can be donated
questions.explanation: Only the hydrogen of the −COOH group is donated, so ethanoic acid is monoprotic. The three hydrogens bonded to carbon are not acidic, and there is only one hydrogen bonded to oxygen.

questions.stem: What is meant by a polyprotic acid?
options: An acid that ionises completely in water
An acid that can donate more than one proton per molecule
An acid that is made of more than one type of molecule
An acid that can accept more than one proton per molecule
questions.explanation: A polyprotic acid, such as sulfuric acid (diprotic) or phosphoric acid (triprotic), can donate more than one H⁺ per molecule. Ionising completely describes a strong acid.

questions.stem: What is an alkali?
options: A base that dissolves in water
An acid that dissolves in water
Any salt that dissolves in water
A base that does not dissolve in water
questions.explanation: Soluble bases are called alkalis, such as sodium hydroxide and ammonia. Insoluble bases, such as copper(II) oxide, are still bases but not alkalis.

questions.stem: A solution has a pH of 3. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Solutions with a pH below 7 at 25 °C are acidic, pH 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic. A pH of 3 is typical of vinegar.

questions.stem: Solution P has pH 2 and solution Q has pH 5. Which statement is correct?
options: P and Q have the same concentration of hydrogen ions
Q is more acidic than P because its pH value is larger
P has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions than Q
Q has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions than P
questions.explanation: pH depends on the concentration of hydrogen ions: the lower the pH, the higher the H⁺ concentration and the more acidic the solution. A larger pH value means a less acidic solution.

questions.stem: Which list is in order of increasing pH?
options: Household ammonia, pure water, lemon juice
Pure water, lemon juice, household ammonia
Lemon juice, household ammonia, pure water
Lemon juice, pure water, household ammonia
questions.explanation: Lemon juice is acidic (pH about 2), pure water is neutral (pH 7), and household ammonia is basic (pH about 11). Increasing pH runs from acidic to basic.

questions.stem: Equal volumes of 1 mol/L sulfuric acid and 1 mol/L hydrochloric acid are each neutralised with sodium hydroxide. Why does the sulfuric acid need twice as much sodium hydroxide?
options: Sulfuric acid is diprotic, so each molecule donates two protons
Sulfuric acid is a stronger acid, so it ionises more completely
Sulfuric acid has a larger molar mass, so it contains more acid
Sulfuric acid is more concentrated, so it has more molecules
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, while HCl reacts 1 : 1. The two solutions contain the same number of acid molecules, but each sulfuric acid molecule can donate two protons.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a strong acid from a weak acid?
options: A strong acid is concentrated; a weak acid is dilute
A strong acid has a high pH; a weak acid has a low pH
A strong acid is polyprotic; a weak acid is monoprotic
A strong acid ionises completely in water; a weak acid ionises only partly
questions.explanation: Strength describes how completely an acid donates protons: HCl ionises completely and ethanoic acid only partly. Concentration is a separate idea, the amount of acid per litre.

questions.stem: Which description fits 10 mol/L ethanoic acid?
questions.explanation: 10 mol/L is a high concentration, so the solution is concentrated, but ethanoic acid ionises only partly, so it is weak. Strong and concentrated are independent properties.

questions.stem: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are both 0.10 mol/L. Which statement about them is correct?
options: Both have the same pH, because their concentrations are equal
The ethanoic acid has a lower pH, because it has more hydrogen atoms
The hydrochloric acid has a higher pH, because it is diprotic
The hydrochloric acid has a lower pH, because it ionises completely
questions.explanation: At equal concentration, the strong acid HCl ionises completely and gives a higher H⁺ concentration, so a lower pH. Ethanoic acid ionises only slightly, and its extra hydrogens bonded to carbon are not acidic.

questions.stem: What are the products when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid?
options: Zinc chloride, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. Water forms with bases, and carbon dioxide forms with carbonates.

questions.stem: What is the balanced equation for the reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Calcium forms Ca²⁺, so the salt is CaCl₂ and two HCl are needed to balance the equation.

questions.stem: What are the products of the reaction between sodium hydrogen carbonate and ethanoic acid?
options: Sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: A hydrogen carbonate reacts with an acid like a carbonate, giving a salt, water and carbon dioxide: NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. The fizzing seen when bicarbonate soda meets vinegar is the carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid. What are the products?
questions.explanation: A metal oxide is a base, and acid + base → salt + water: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. Hydrogen forms only when an acid reacts with a reactive metal.

questions.stem: Which ionic equation represents the neutralisation of any strong acid by a hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: In every reaction between a strong acid and a hydroxide, H⁺ ions combine with OH⁻ ions to form water. The other ions, such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻, are spectators.

questions.stem: A white powder fizzes when dilute hydrochloric acid is added, and the gas turns limewater milky. A grey solid also fizzes with the acid, but its gas burns with a squeaky pop. What are the two solids most likely to be?
options: A metal hydroxide and a metal carbonate
A metal oxide and a metal hydroxide
A metal carbonate and a reactive metal
A metal hydroxide and a reactive metal
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (limewater test) comes from an acid reacting with a carbonate, and hydrogen (squeaky pop) comes from an acid reacting with a reactive metal. Hydroxides and oxides are neutralised without producing any gas.

questions.stem: A white solid dissolves in dilute nitric acid with no bubbling, and the solution warms slightly. Which type of compound is the solid most likely to be?
questions.explanation: A metal hydroxide neutralises the acid to give a salt and water, releasing heat but no gas. Carbonates and hydrogen carbonates would release carbon dioxide, and a reactive metal would release hydrogen.

questions.stem: 25.0 mL of 2.00 mol/L hydrochloric acid is diluted with water to a total volume of 250 mL. What is the new concentration?
questions.explanation: Dilution does not change the amount of acid: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂, so c₂ = 2.00 × 25.0/250 = 0.200 mol/L. Diluting must lower the concentration, which rules out 20.0.

questions.stem: What volume of 10.0 mol/L sulfuric acid is needed to make 500 mL of 0.500 mol/L sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: V₁ = c₂V₂/c₁ = 0.500 × 500/10.0 = 25.0 mL. The concentrated acid is then added to water and made up to 500 mL.

questions.stem: Which statement about diluting a solution is correct?
options: The number of moles of solute increases as water is added
The number of moles of solute stays the same, but the volume increases
The number of moles of solute decreases as water is added
The concentration increases because there is more liquid present
questions.explanation: Adding water spreads the same amount of solute through a larger volume, so the concentration falls. This is why c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ can be used.

questions.stem: Which description defines the equivalence point of an acid-base titration?
options: The point at which the burette has been emptied completely
The point at which the solution in the flask first begins to fizz
The point at which the pH of the solution reaches 14
The point at which the acid and base have reacted in the exact mole ratio of the equation
questions.explanation: At the equivalence point the reactants have been mixed in exactly the amounts shown by the balanced equation. It is detected by an indicator colour change (the endpoint) or by a sharp change in pH on a pH meter.

questions.stem: In a titration, 20.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide exactly neutralises 25.0 mL of hydrochloric acid. What is the concentration of the acid?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol, and HCl reacts 1 : 1, so c(HCl) = 0.00200/0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/L. Swapping the two volumes gives 0.125.

questions.stem: 25.0 mL of sulfuric acid needs 30.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide for neutralisation. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the acid?
A 20.0 mL aliquot of 0.0500 mol/L sodium carbonate is titrated with hydrochloric acid, and the titre is 16.0 mL. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. What is the concentration of the acid?
Before a titration, what should the burette be rinsed with?
options: Distilled water only, and then left wet
The solution that will be placed in the flask
Tap water, and then dried with a paper towel
The solution it is about to be filled with
questions.explanation: Rinsing with the solution it will hold means any liquid left on the walls does not dilute or contaminate the titrant. Leaving water inside would dilute it and make the titre too large.
